notes: Bail judicial review after abolition of High Court bail applications; jurisdiction confirmed but refusal upheld as not Wednesbury unreasonable.

enrichment.short_title: M v Isleworth Crown Court: judicial review of Crown Court bail refusal
key_facts: M, a 55-year-old Heathrow baggage handler of good character, was charged with four conspiracies to import class A cocaine allegedly on accomplice evidence from W.
HHJ Katkhuda refused bail at Isleworth Crown Court in November 2004 despite strong personal mitigation and a weak-looking prosecution case.
Section 17(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 had abolished direct High Court bail applications from 5 April 2004.
M sought judicial review of the Crown Court refusal, arguing the decision was perverse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review treated substantively in the Administrative Court after abolition of the former High Court bail route.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and the application heard substantively, but the bail refusal was upheld as not irrational or perverse; the application was dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Following abolition of direct High Court bail applications, prerogative remedies under section 17(6)(b) of the 2003 Act permit judicial review of Crown Court bail decisions, but only very sparingly on robust Wednesbury principles; a refusal of bail in serious drug importation cases with a real absconding risk is not perverse merely because a High Court judge might have granted conditional bail.
legal_issues: Whether a Crown Court bail decision is excluded from judicial review as relating to trial on indictment
Whether refusal of bail remains susceptible to judicial review after abolition of the High Court bail remedy
Whether the circuit judge's refusal was Wednesbury unreasonable or perverse
linked_authorities: R v Manchester Crown Court ex parte DPP [1994] 98 Cr App R 461
R v Croydon Crown Court ex parte Cox [1997] 1 Cr App R 20
Serumaga [2005] EWCA Crim 370

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional analysis and final disposition are clearly reasoned, though the court emphasised sparing use of the remedy.

notes: Pirelli limitation accrual point preserved on indistinguishable hotel bay-window facts; Murphy did not impliedly overrule Pirelli.

enrichment.short_title: Abbott v Will Gannon: Pirelli limitation and negligent building design
key_facts: Hotel owners in Torquay retained consulting engineers in 1995 to design remedial works to a bay window; the work was completed in March 1997.
Cracking appeared in late 1999 and further remedial works costing about £20,000 were required.
Proceedings issued in September 2003 were time-barred if the cause of action accrued on completion in 1997 but not if it accrued when physical damage first occurred.
The engineers argued Murphy v Brentwood displaced Pirelli and that economic loss accrued on completion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal transferred under CPR 52.14 from Exeter County Court where limitation was tried as a preliminary issue on agreed facts.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the court held itself bound by Pirelli and Ketteman, and alternatively that loss accrued in 1999 on an Invercargill-style analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Absent express overruling by the House of Lords, Pirelli remains binding: in negligent design cases a cause of action for latent building defects accrues when physical damage first occurs, not when defective work is completed; Lord Keith's observations in Murphy do not impliedly overrule Pirelli.
legal_issues: Whether Murphy v Brentwood overruled Pirelli on accrual of limitation periods
Whether economic loss on completion or physical damage governs accrual where there is a special relationship
Whether insurer letters amounted to an admission precluding the limitation defence
linked_authorities: Pirelli General Cable Works Ltd v Oscar Faber & Partners [1983] 2 AC 1
Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991] AC 398
Ketteman v Hansel Properties Ltd [1987] AC 189
Invercargill City Council v Hamlin [1996] AC 624

confidence.notes: Limitation issue and binding authority analysis are explicit, though Tuckey LJ acknowledged residual uncertainty in the wider law.

notes: Attorney General reference on indecent assault of child; extended sentence not interfered with despite short custodial term.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 142 of 2004: indecent assault extended sentence
key_facts: A 32-year-old offender was convicted after trial of four indecent assaults and one indecency with a child against a 10-year-old friend of his stepdaughter over 18 months.
Conduct included touching the child's vagina, kissing, masturbation and pressing his penis against her without penetration.
He was sentenced to an extended sentence with a 2-year custodial term plus 2-year extended licence and 3 months consecutive for a Bail Act offence.
Semen on a sweatshirt corroborated the victim; the offender maintained innocence and had no prior sexual convictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted but the court declined to interfere, finding the custodial term lenient but doubting whether the total extended sentence was unduly lenient.
enrichment.ratio: For repeated indecent assaults on a vulnerable child in a position of trust, a trial judge might properly impose about three years' custody; where an extended licence period is added, the court may exercise its discretion not to increase an otherwise lenient custodial term.
legal_issues: Whether a 2-year custodial term was unduly lenient for sustained indecent assault of a child
Relevance of breach of trust, repetition and touching of the vagina
Whether the extended licence period rendered the overall sentence adequate
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 20 of 1998 (R v Pidcock) [1999] 1 Cr App R(S) 280
Attorney-General's Reference No 32 of 1998 (R v Gilks) [1999] 1 Cr App R(S) 316
R v Simpson 12 Cr App R(S) 674

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating features and discretionary non-interference are clearly recorded.

notes: Secure tenancy possession appeal; late new evidence failed all Ladd v Marshall hurdles after sub-letting trial.

enrichment.short_title: Brent v Smart: secure tenancy and Ladd v Marshall new evidence
key_facts: Mr Smart held a secure tenancy from Brent since 1983 at Lansbury Close, NW10.
Brent brought possession proceedings alleging he sub-let the whole flat to Miss Thomas in 2000 via a fraudulent tenancy agreement through Callams estate agents.
At trial HHJ Levy preferred Miss Thomas's evidence and found a whole flat sub-letting destroying the secure tenancy under section 93(2).
Mr Smart lost legal aid shortly before trial and sought to rely on late witness evidence on appeal, including from a former lover of Miss Thomas.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a possession order after a four-day trial, principally on admission of new evidence under Ladd v Marshall.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the new evidence failed the Ladd v Marshall tests and was not otherwise required in the interests of justice; stay of execution lifted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tenant's defence at trial was already that the sub-letting documents were fraudulent and the judge accepted the landlord's witness, late new evidence must satisfy Ladd v Marshall strictly; evidence obtained shortly before appeal without satisfactory explanation and lacking credibility will not justify a retrial.
legal_issues: Whether new evidence was unavailable at trial with reasonable diligence
Whether new evidence would probably have an important influence on the result
Whether new evidence was apparently credible
Whether it was reasonable to make a possession order on the facts found
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489
Hertfordshire Investments Ltd v Bubb [2000] 1 WLR 2318
Hamilton v Al Fayed (21 December 2000, unreported)

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings on new evidence and explicit application of Ladd v Marshall.

notes: Long-running Egger chipboard factory GMP dispute; SCL net winner and awarded 55% of costs after conduct analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Skanska v Egger: construction dispute costs after GMP factory project

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Skanska Construction UK transformed a redundant Ayrshire colliery into an automated Egger chipboard factory under a £12 million guaranteed maximum price contract.
Disputes over variations, delay, final account and counterclaims generated litigation costs of about £9 million over many years.
Separate liability and quantum trials followed two preliminary issues on contract formation and insurance.
SCL recovered about £5.4 million including interest but net about £2.88 million after counterclaims; both parties' conduct was criticised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court judgment on costs after liability and quantum trials in a complex final-account and loss-and-expense dispute.
enrichment.outcome: SCL was the overall net winner; Egger was ordered to pay 55% of SCL's costs, reflecting shared litigation misconduct and partial success on claims and counterclaims.
enrichment.ratio: In multi-issue construction litigation the successful party is primarily the one receiving a net monetary payment; under CPR Part 44.3 conduct, exaggeration and intransigence on both sides may justify a percentage costs order rather than full recovery, especially where neither party made Part 36 offers.
legal_issues: Who was the successful party where both claim and counterclaim succeeded in part
Effect of parties' pre-litigation and trial conduct on costs discretion
Whether interest should be treated as part of recovery for costs purposes
Appropriateness of a percentage rather than issue-based costs order

confidence.notes: Final net recovery figures and 55% costs order are explicit, though the underlying quantum history is extremely lengthy.

notes: CIF Jeddah shipment with prohibited transhipment; SABO knew of feeder voyage and bill misrepresented voyage to bank.

enrichment.short_title: SABo v UASC: transhipment, letter of credit and misrepresentation
key_facts: SABO contracted to supply brick-making plant CIF Jeddah under a letter of credit prohibiting transhipment and requiring clean on-board bills of lading.
UASC arranged feeder carriage from Piraeus to Gioia Tauro on the Carl Metz for transhipment onto the Al Sabahia to Jeddah.
SABO and Hellenic agreed bills naming the ocean vessel only so documents would conform to the credit despite planned transhipment.
The Carl Metz stranded at Gioia Tauro causing cargo damage; insurers declined cover and Makkah rejected documents; SABO supplied replacement goods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of SABO's claim for misrepresentation and breach of contract and UASC's counterclaim for container charges.
enrichment.outcome: SABO's claim failed; UASC did not misrepresent to SABO, which was privy to the documentary misrepresentation intended for the bank; UASC's counterclaim also failed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a shipper knowingly accepts transhipment via a hub port while procuring bills of lading showing direct carriage on the ocean vessel, any misrepresentation in the bill is not actionable by the shipper against the carrier; the contract contemplated feeder carriage agreed between the parties.
legal_issues: Whether UASC misrepresented that cargo would be shipped directly from Piraeus to Jeddah
Whether SABO relied on representations about transhipment
Whether UASC breached the contract by using a feeder vessel
Whether UASC could recover container rental and storage from SABO after the casualty

confidence.notes: Findings on meeting evidence, customs documents and second shipment are detailed and conclusive.

notes: Stolen-books fence exemplary damages upheld in Rookes second category despite parallel confiscation proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Borders v Jordan: exemplary damages for stolen book handling
key_facts: Ronald Jordan sold large quantities of new books stolen by shoplifters from major retailers through market stalls, making substantial profits.
About 46,780 seized books were identified; compensatory damages of £279,594.89 were awarded for conversion and tracing costs.
Master Leslie additionally awarded £100,000 exemplary damages for profits on unrecovered stolen stock.
Jordan was imprisoned for conspiracy and handling; confiscation proceedings were adjourned pending the civil appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from assessment of damages by a master after default judgment, challenging an exemplary damages award.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the £100,000 award was upheld as falling within Lord Devlin's second Rookes category despite being quantified by reference to unrecovered losses.
enrichment.ratio: Exemplary damages remain available where a defendant cynically persists in tort calculated to profit beyond likely recovery; quantification reflecting actual unrecovered losses does not necessarily convert the award into compensatory damages, and coexistence with criminal confiscation does not automatically bar a civil exemplary award.
legal_issues: Whether exemplary and compensatory damages are mutually exclusive
Whether quantified profit-based awards can be exemplary
Interaction between exemplary damages and confiscation under the Criminal Justice Act 1988
Whether the claim should have been pleaded as additional compensatory damages
linked_authorities: Rookes v Barnard [1964] AC 1129
Kuddus v Chief Constable of the Leicestershire Constabulary [2002] 2 AC 122
Attorney General v Blake [2001] 1 AC 268
Cassell & Co Ltd v Broome [1972] AC 1027

confidence.notes: Master's calculations and Court of Appeal reasoning on Rookes category two are thorough.

notes: Underage alcohol sale due diligence appeal; magistrates' case stated inadequate on positive training evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Davies v Carmarthenshire: due diligence defence for underage alcohol sale
key_facts: The appellant manageress and Mr Bailes were joint licensees of a Spar store in Kidwelly.
Sales assistant Hayley Fisher sold Red Square vodka to a 15-year-old in a Trading Standards test purchase on 16 July 2003.
Fisher pleaded guilty; the licensees relied on the section 169(4)(b) due diligence defence.
The company had till prompts, handbooks, notices and training materials, and Fisher had previously refused underage sales.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Dyfed Powys magistrates who rejected the due diligence defence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the question whether the justices were entitled to reject due diligence was answered in the negative; costs from central funds ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where adequate employer systems exist, a line manager charged by reason of an employee's default may establish due diligence by proving proactive implementation of training and supervision; a case stated that ignores undisputed positive compliance material and focuses only on negative impressions of the manager may be flawed.
legal_issues: Whether the appellant exercised all due diligence to prevent an underage sale by her employee
Adequacy of company systems versus breakdown in local implementation
Whether the magistrates' case stated sufficiently reflected agreed positive evidence

confidence.notes: Undisputed training materials and till mechanisms are clearly identified; outcome turns on inadequacy of case stated reasoning.

notes: Historic stepdaughter abuse conviction quashed; section 41 wrongly excluded adult relationship videos and photos.

enrichment.short_title: R v Flint: section 41 and adult relationship evidence

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Flint was convicted of specimen counts of rape and gross indecency against his stepdaughter alleged to have occurred from age 7 to 16.
The complainant and appellant agreed they later had a consensual adult sexual relationship from about 1991 to 1995/6.
The judge allowed evidence of the adult relationship but excluded videos and holiday photographs showing enthusiastic participation.
The complainant said she submitted through fear; the appellant said she initiated the relationship and later made false allegations for revenge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal Criminal Division appeal against conviction after trial before HHJ de Mille.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed, convictions quashed and a new trial ordered; exclusion of videos and photographs rendered the verdict unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 41, where the fact of an adult relationship is admissible because it is relevant to whether childhood abuse occurred and to alleged motive, the court cannot then exclude objective evidence capable of rebutting the complainant's account of submission once admissibility criteria are met; section 41 is not a general discretion to limit relevant defence evidence.
legal_issues: Admissibility of complainant sexual history under section 41(3) where consent is not in issue
Application of section 41(5) to rebut prosecution evidence about the adult relationship
Whether exclusion of videos and photographs rendered the conviction unsafe
Whether the judge had discretion to exclude relevant evidence to avoid humiliation
linked_authorities: R v Martin [2004] EWCA Crim 916

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of section 41 and explicit quashing order with new trial direction.

notes: Dr Krippendorf GMC permission application dismissed on all three grounds; costs awarded in exceptional circumstances.

enrichment.short_title: Krippendorf v GMC: permission refused on fitness to practise challenges
key_facts: Dr Krippendorf challenged the GMC registrar's referral of a misconduct complaint to a screener in June 2004.
She also sought recognition of specialist German qualifications and enforcement of a 2000 Privy Council order quashing a CPP suspension.
Proceedings were begun by appellant's notice but treated as an application for permission to apply for judicial review.
The GMC argued the complaints were hopeless, out of time, or not yet final decisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review in the Administrative Court of three GMC decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on all grounds; application dismissed; exceptional costs of £4,630 summarily assessed against the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: The registrar need only refer a complaint to a screener if a question of serious professional misconduct arises, not decide merits; stale qualification and Privy Council enforcement challenges brought years late are not viable judicial review targets; hopeless permission applications pursued after clear defendant responses may attract costs under Mount Cook.
legal_issues: Whether the registrar erred in referring a complaint to a screener
Whether refusal to recognise German qualifications was susceptible to judicial review
Effect of the Privy Council quashing a CPP determination on immediate suspension under section 38
Whether costs should be awarded at the permission stage
linked_authorities: Krippendorf v General Medical Council (Privy Council Appeal No 43 of 1999)

confidence.notes: Each ground is addressed separately with clear refusal reasons and a costs ruling.
